units.title: The Endocrine System
units.intro:
**Exocrine** glands have ducts (sweat, saliva). **Endocrine** glands are ductless — hormones go straight into blood and hunt a *target organ*. Compared with nerves: hormones are slower and last longer (growth, metabolism, cycles).

A gland fires when nerves poke it, or when another hormone pokes it (the pituitary is the usual “boss”).

cards.title: 1.1.1 The Pituitary Gland
body: The pituitary gland is a small, bean-shaped gland located in the lower part of the brain.
The pituitary gland is structurally and functionally divided into two major lobes.
The growth hormone (GH), or somatotropic hormone, promotes normal skeletal and muscular growth by regulating cell division, protein synthesis, and bone growth.
Prolactin causes the mammary glands in breasts to develop and produce milk in women who are breastfeeding.

cards.title: 1.1.2 The Thyroid Gland
body: The human thyroid gland is a butterfly-shaped gland, located at the base of the neck in front of the trachea (windpipe).
The thyroid gland is critical to the healthy development and maturation of vertebrates, and regulates metabolism.
The thyroid gland secretes thyroxine and calcitonin hormones.
Iodine is an essential component of thyroxine, and its synthesis requires iodine to be present in the diet.

cards.title: 1.1.3 The Parathyroid Glands
body: Parathyroid (para – meaning beside) glands are usually four small, flattened glands which are located behind the thyroid gland.
The parathyroid glands secrete a parathyroid hormone (PTH), or parathormone, that controls the concentration of calcium ions in the blood.
The correct amounts of calcium ions in the bloodstream are necessary for muscle contraction, nerve impulse transmission, bone and teeth development, blood clotting and other tasks.
When the concentration of calcium ions in the blood decreases, PTH activates bone cells to release calcium and phosphate ions, and stimulates the kidneys to conserve them.

cards.title: 1.1.4 The Adrenal Glands
body: The adrenal cortex is the bulky, outer portion of the gland and secretes many steroid hormones, collectively known as corticosteroids, or corticoids.
Corticosteroids fall into three categories: glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids and sex steroids.
Glucocorticoids regulate metabolism (fat and protein), help the body adapt to stress, and repair damaged tissues.
One of the most important glucocorticoid hormones is cortisol, which increases the metabolic rate of fats, proteins and carbohydrates.

cards.title: 1.1.5 The Pancreas
body: Exocrine cells secrete digestive juices or pancreatic juices.
Scattered through the pancreas are groups of endocrine cells called the islets of Langerhans.
The islets of Langerhans constantly monitor the amount of glucose in the blood.
Insulin triggers the liver to convert excess glucose into glycogen.

cards.title: 1.1.6 The Sex Glands
body: Gamete production also takes place in these sex glands.
The human reproductive system consists of a pair of primary reproductive organs (gonads), accessory glands and ducts.
The male has two oval gonads, called testes, and the female has two gonads, called ovaries.
The testes contain endocrine tissue referred to as Leydig cells (interstitial cells).

cards.title: 1.1.7 The Thymus Gland
body: The size of the thymus varies considerably from person to person; however, the thymus gland is relatively large in newborns and children, and sharply decreases in size after puberty.
In adults, the gland gradually degenerates (shrinks) until it almost disappears.
The thymus gland therefore is functional primarily in childhood.
White blood cells multiply, differentiate and mature in this gland.

cards.title: 1.1.8 The Pineal gland
body: The pineal (“pinealis” meaning “shaped like a pine cone”) gland is a small mass; a cone-shaped tissue located in the brain.
The pineal gland contains cells that are light sensitive (photosensitive).
The blood levels of melatonin therefore vary from day to night, and they also change according to the season (spring, summer, autumn, winter).
Melatonin controls skin pigmentation (colour).

cards.problem: Which of the following describes the mechanism of secretion of an endocrine gland compared to an exocrine gland?

steps.text: **Step 1: Understand gland anatomy**
Endocrine glands are ductless glands that release their secretions, called hormones, directly into the surrounding interstitial fluid and blood vessels.
Exocrine glands, such as sweat and salivary glands, possess ducts that carry their secretions to a body surface or cavity.
**Step 2: Evaluate options**
The option correctly specifying that endocrine glands secrete directly into the bloodstream and exocrine glands use ducts is the accurate description.

cards.answer: Endocrine glands secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream, whereas exocrine glands secrete substances through ducts.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Hormone target specificity is determined by which of the following cellular features?

steps.text: **Step 1: Define hormone-receptor binding**
Hormones circulate throughout the entire body via the blood, but only affect cells that express specific protein receptors that can bind that hormone.
**Step 2: Relate to cell characteristics**
Cells without these specialized receptors are blind to the hormonal signal, making receptor presence the key factor in specificity.
**Step 3: Final Result**

cards.answer: The presence of unique protein receptors on or inside the target cell

units.intro: **Primary** characters = the gonads and genitalia you are born with. **Secondary** = puberty changes (voice, hair, breasts, hips) driven by sex hormones.

Reproduction is important in ensuring the continuity of life and/or the species.
Reproduction also increases the number of individuals of a species.
In asexual reproduction only one parent produces offspring of the same genetic makeup.
Part or parts of an organism break off to produce more of the same kind, or the organism divides into two or more parts.

Primary sexual characteristics refer to the anatomical structures directly involved in reproduction that are present at birth.

cards.title: 2.2 The Male Reproductive System
body: The male reproductive system consists of the testes, epididymis, vas deferens, urethra, seminal vesicles, Cowper’s gland, prostate gland, scrotum, and penis.
Testes: Testes, also called testicles, are the primary sex organs (gonads) of the male reproductive system.
The two testes are positioned outside the body cavity, one at either side of the penis.
The testes are ovoid structures about five centimetres in length and three centimetres in diameter.
Testes are the site in which the sperm cells (spermatozoa) and male sex hormones are produced.

body: Ovary (egg + oestrogen/progesterone) → oviduct (fertilisation address) → uterus (implants) → cervix → vagina.

cards.title: Cycle — 28-day story
body: FSH grows a follicle; oestrogen rebuilds the uterus lining; LH surge ~day 14 ovulates; corpus luteum makes progesterone to keep the lining; if no embryo, progesterone falls and the lining is shed (menstruation).

cards.title: Mnemonic — FOLP
body: FSH → Oestrogen → LH → Progesterone. “First Open the Lining, then Protect it.”

cards.title: Cycle — 28-day story
body: **Fertilisation** in the oviduct. Zygote → blastocyst implants. Placenta feeds and exchanges gases; amniotic sac cushions. Birth: oxytocin (posterior pituitary) helps contractions.

**Contraception** in the book: barrier, hormonal (stop ovulation), IUD, natural / calendar (least reliable), sterilisation. Exam: name the method and the *how* (block sperm / stop egg / stop implant).

cards.title: 2.3.1 Menstruation
body: After ovulation, if the ovum is fertilized by a sperm cell, a zygote is formed.
The corpus luteum produces progesterone, a hormone which causes the thickening of the uterine wall, in preparation to receive the fertilized ovum.
The endometrial wall and the unfertilized ovum is discharged with blood from the vagina.
After menstruation, the uterine lining begins to build up again.

cards.title: 2.3.2 Hormonal Control of Reproduction
body: Reproductive processes are controlled by a variety of hormones.
The hormonal mechanisms that influence the reproductive system involve the hypothalamus, pituitary gland, testes and ovaries.
The hypothalamus of the brain produces a chemical substance, such as the gonadotropin-releasing hormone (Gn-RH) that travels to the pituitary gland.
Before puberty a small amount of testosterone and other androgens are available in the male’s body.

cards.title: 2.3.3 Fertilization and Pregnancy
body: Ovulation occurs roughly every 28 days, where one ovum is released alternatively by each of the two ovaries.
By ciliary action of the cells lining the fallopian tube, the ovum travels down the tube, where it may become fertilized by a sperm cell.
The ovum lives for only about 24 hours after it is released from the ovary.
During sexual intercourse or copulation, three to five million sperm cells per cubic centimetre of semen are released.

cards.title: 2.3.4 Child birth
body: Towards the end of gestation, the thick wall of the uterus begins to undergo regular powerful contractions, or labour.
The abdominal wall contracts; eventually the amnion is broken and amniotic fluid flows out through the vagina.
The fetus, with its head lying towards the cervix, gradually emerges through the vagina.
The portion of the umbilical cord remaining in the mother and the placenta are forced out by contractions of the abdominal and uterine walls.

cards.title: 5.3.2 The Liver and Sugar Control

cards.title: 6.3.1 Tap and Fibrous Root Systems
body: The two principal functions of roots are the absorption of water and minerals, and anchorage.
When the seed germinates, the radicle is usually the first structure to appear; it becomes the first root and is called the primary root.
In many plants (e.g. beet, radish and carrot), the primary root remains the principal root throughout the life of the plant.
The development of a fibrous root system (like that of barley or wheat) is different from that of a tap root system.

cards.title: 6.3.2 Root Growth Regions
body: Root Cap: The root cap is made up of parenchyma cells that form an inverted cup-shape, as a covering for the tip of each root.
The outer part of the root cap is rough and uneven because its cells are constantly being worn away as the root pushes through the soil.
The main function of the root cap is to protect the delicate root tip.
The growing point also gives rise to new root cap cells to replace the ones that have worn away.

cards.title: 6.3.3 Internal Structure of the Root
body: In cross section, a root has an epidermis, cortex, endodermis and pericycle, and xylem and phloem.
The cortex is the tissue immediately inside the epidermis and functions in storing food.
The innermost layer of the cortex is the endodermis.
Inside the endodermis is a cylinder of parenchyma cells called the pericycle.

body: The leaf is the site of food production in plants.

Monocots and dicots are distinguished on the basis of leaf structure.
Monocots have typically simple leaves with parallel venation, while dicots have branching venation.

cards.title: 6.4.3 The Flower: Structure and Function
body: The flower is the part of the shoot system specially modified for reproduction.
In a typical flower there are four sets of floral parts arranged in rings or whorls.
From the outside of the flower towards the centre, the four sets of floral parts are distinguished as the calyx, corolla, gynoecium and androecium.

Water in the xylem moves up from the roots to the stem and leaves by the action of root pressure and transpiration pull.
Root pressure is one of the forces that push water up the xylem.
The pulling force set up by the evaporation of water from the leaves is called transpiration pull.
